An ANR fires when the main thread fails to respond in time — roughly five seconds for an input event.

### The system raises one when
- An input event has not been handled within about 5 seconds.
- A BroadcastReceiver has not returned within ~10s in the foreground or ~60s in the background.
- A service started with `startForegroundService` does not call `startForeground` within its timeout.
- `Service.onCreate` / `onStartCommand` or a ContentProvider call overruns.

### Avoid them by never blocking the main thread
- Move I/O, database work and heavy CPU off main with coroutines and `Dispatchers.IO` / `Default`.
- No `Thread.sleep`, no `runBlocking`, no `.get()` on a future on the main thread.
- Watch for the blocking calls that do not look blocking: synchronous IPC (`Binder.transact`), the first SharedPreferences read, a Room query accidentally left non-suspend, inflating a huge layout, decoding a bitmap during scroll.
- Turn on `StrictMode` in debug builds so disk and network on main fail loudly while you develop.
- Profile with a system trace (Perfetto, from the Android Studio profiler) and look at the worst frames, not the average.

Diagnose in production with Play Console Vitals, which gives the main-thread stack at the moment of the timeout, and read `ApplicationExitInfo` on the next launch to find out why the previous process died — it reports ANRs, crashes and low-memory kills with the trace attached.

A leak on Android is almost always something long-lived holding on to a destroyed Activity, Fragment or View.

### Where they come from
- A static field or singleton holding a `Context` — pass `applicationContext` to anything that outlives a screen.
- Inner classes and lambdas capturing `this` — a delayed `Handler` callback, a listener, a Runnable.
- Listeners registered with a system service, an event bus or a third-party SDK and never unregistered.
- Fragments keeping a `View`, a view binding or an adapter past `onDestroyView` — the fragment outlives its view tree, so the binding must be nulled there.
- Coroutines in `GlobalScope`, or a `CoroutineScope` you created yourself and never cancelled.
- Large bitmaps and drawables cached in a static field.

### Find them
- **LeakCanary in debug builds** — it watches destroyed Activities, Fragments, ViewModels and Services, and when one stays reachable it prints the exact reference chain holding it.
- **Android Studio's Memory Profiler** — rotate a screen a few times, capture a heap dump, and look for more than one instance of the same Activity.
- `adb shell dumpsys meminfo <package>` for a quick size check, and Play Vitals for real-user OOM rates.

Fix by shortening lifetimes rather than sprinkling `WeakReference`: scope work to `viewModelScope` / `lifecycleScope`, unregister in the matching lifecycle callback, use `DisposableEffect` in Compose, and keep state in a ViewModel that is cleared for you.

Jank is a frame that misses its deadline, so the display shows the previous one again and the user sees a stutter.

The budget is one refresh interval — about 16.7ms at 60Hz, 8.3ms at 120Hz — shared between your main-thread work and the RenderThread.

### Measure
- **While developing** — a system trace (Perfetto) from the Android Studio profiler. Every frame is a slice on the frame timeline, janky ones are flagged, and you can see which call overran.
- **In CI** — Macrobenchmark with `FrameTimingMetric`, which reports P50/P90/P99 frame durations for a scripted journey, so a regression fails the build instead of shipping.
- **In production** — the `JankStats` library reports per-frame durations from real devices, tagged with the state you attach (which screen was on top).
- **Quick check** — `adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo <package> framestats`.

### Common causes and fixes
- Work on the main thread during scroll: image decoding, JSON parsing, disk reads. Move it off and prefetch before the row is visible.
- **Compose** — reading state too high in the tree so a whole screen recomposes; unstable parameters that defeat skipping; allocating in a composable. Defer reads into lambdas (`Modifier.offset { }`, `graphicsLayer`), hoist state no higher than it needs to go, give `LazyColumn` items a stable `key`, and check the recomposition counts in Layout Inspector.
- **Views** — deep hierarchies and overdraw. Flatten with ConstraintLayout, drop redundant backgrounds, and use `DiffUtil` with stable ids so RecyclerView rebinds only what changed.
- The first frames of a screen running interpreted instead of compiled — that is what a baseline profile fixes.

R8 shrinks, optimizes and obfuscates your code in a single pass over the bytecode when you build a release variant. It replaced ProGuard as the default years ago, so `minifyEnabled` today means R8.

### What it does
- **Shrinking** — walks the reference graph from the entry points named in the manifest and drops every class, method and field nothing reaches.
- **Optimization** — inlining, dead-code elimination, class merging, devirtualization, constant folding, all whole-program.
- **Obfuscation** — renames what survives to short names, which shrinks the DEX further and makes casual reverse-engineering harder.
- Resource shrinking (`shrinkResources`) — removes drawables and strings no surviving code references.

Full mode is the default in current AGP: R8 optimizes more aggressively and assumes less about reflection than the old ProGuard-compatibility mode, so a library that used to work may now need explicit keep rules.

What breaks is anything resolved by name at runtime — reflection, JNI lookups, `Class.forName`, Gson's field names, class names sent to analytics. Those survive only if a rule keeps them. Most libraries ship consumer rules and need nothing from you, so when a release build crashes and the debug build does not, a missing `-keep` is the first suspect. Keep rules are also the reason a release APK can be larger than it should be: `-keep class com.app.** { *; }` disables shrinking for your whole app.

Always test the release variant before shipping, and upload `mapping.txt` to Play or Crashlytics — without it every production stack trace reads `a.b.c`.

A baseline profile lists the methods ART should compile ahead of time at install, instead of interpreting them on first run.

Without one, a fresh install runs your code interpreted and JIT-compiles it as it goes, so the first launch and the first scroll are the slowest the app will ever be. Google measures roughly 30% faster cold start and visibly smoother first scrolls on real apps.

### How you get one
- Add the `androidx.baselineprofile` Gradle plugin and a benchmark module.
- Write a `BaselineProfileRule` test that drives the critical journeys — launch, scroll the main list, open a detail screen.
- Run `./gradlew :app:generateBaselineProfile` on a rooted emulator or an unlocked device; the plugin writes the rules into the app module and AGP packages them into the APK or AAB.
- **Verify with Macrobenchmark**: measure `StartupTimingMetric` with `CompilationMode.None()` against `CompilationMode.Partial()` and compare, rather than trusting that it helped.

`includeInStartupProfile = true` additionally produces a startup profile, which lets AGP reorder the DEX so startup classes sit together and fewer pages are faulted in.

Two things to say if asked what it does not do: it changes nothing on a device that has already run the app for a while (ART's own profile takes over), and Play separately distributes a cloud profile aggregated from real users, which combines with yours. Regenerate it when the critical journeys change — a stale profile just precompiles code nobody runs.

Cold start is the case that matters: the process, the Application object and the first Activity all have to be created before anything reaches the screen.

- **Cold** — no process exists. Everything is built from scratch.
- **Warm** — the process is alive, the Activity has to be recreated.
- **Hot** — the Activity is still in memory and is only brought forward.

### Measure
- Logcat prints `Displayed com.app/.MainActivity: +XXXms` for the first frame.
- `adb shell am start -W` reports `TotalTime` for one launch.
- Macrobenchmark with `StartupTimingMetric` gives time-to-initial-display and time-to-full-display across iterations, on a device you choose.
- Play Vitals and Firebase Performance give the real-user distribution, which is where slow devices show up.

### Where the time actually goes
- `Application.onCreate` initializing SDKs. Defer everything not needed for the first frame — the App Startup library, a lazy initializer, or work posted after the first frame.
- **ContentProviders**: every library that declares one is created before `Application.onCreate`, and you pay for it whether or not you use the library. App Startup exists to collapse them into a single provider.
- Your code running interpreted on first launch — ship a baseline profile.
- Blocking the first frame on data. Use `installSplashScreen()` with `setKeepOnScreenCondition` only while it is genuinely necessary, and call `reportFullyDrawn()` (or `ReportDrawn` in Compose) when real content is up, so the platform and Play measure time-to-full-display correctly instead of stopping at an empty skeleton.
- **Layout work done twice** — a deep view hierarchy, or a Compose screen that recomposes on every intermediate state during load.

A reasonable target: `Application.onCreate` well under 200ms, and the first meaningful frame under a second on a mid-range device.

Battery complaints are almost always work the app does while nobody is looking — wakeups, polling, location, or a wake lock that was never released.

### Where the drain comes from
- A partial wake lock held far longer than the work needs, or a foreground service with no reason to be running.
- Polling instead of push. Each wakeup drags the cellular radio out of idle, and the tail energy of that dwarfs the bytes you transferred.
- Location at high accuracy and high frequency, background location worst of all.
- **Unbatched work**: twenty alarms firing at random times instead of one job the system can group with everyone else's.
- Sensors, Bluetooth scans, and camera or media sessions left running after the screen is off.

### How you find it
- Play Console Vitals flags excessive wakeups, stuck partial wake locks and excessive background network use, with a per-device breakdown.
- `adb shell dumpsys batterystats --reset`, run the scenario, then dump again — or load the result into Battery Historian for a timeline.
- A Perfetto trace with the power and wakeup tracks on a supported device attributes wakeups to your process.
- `adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle` and `am set-standby-bucket` let you test Doze and a restricted bucket instead of hoping.

### Fixes
- Deferrable work goes to WorkManager with constraints, so the system batches it with everyone else's.
- Replace polling with FCM, and reserve high-priority messages for something genuinely user-visible.
- Exact alarms are for user-facing events only; they need a runtime permission and the user can see them.
- Batch analytics and telemetry rather than waking the radio per event.
- Work with Doze and App Standby buckets rather than asking for a battery-optimization exemption, which is a Play policy risk and a review question.

A decoded bitmap costs width times height times bytes per pixel, and nothing about the file size on disk predicts that number.

Do the arithmetic once and it stops being surprising. A 4000x3000 photo is a two-megabyte JPEG, but decoded at `ARGB_8888` it is 48 MB of pixels. Three of those on screen at once exceed the heap limit on plenty of shipping devices, and the crash arrives as an OOM in the decoder rather than anywhere near the code that caused it.

### What fixes it
- Decode at display size, not source size. `inJustDecodeBounds` plus `inSampleSize`, or `ImageDecoder` with `setTargetSize`. In practice Coil or Glide reads the target size for you and downsamples, which is the main reason not to hand-roll image loading.
- Pick the config deliberately. `RGB_565` halves the cost where banding is acceptable; `HARDWARE` keeps pixels in graphics memory off the Java heap, at the price of not being readable pixel by pixel.
- **Cache in two tiers** — an in-memory LRU sized as a fraction of the available heap, plus a disk cache so a scroll back up does not hit the network.
- Cancel in-flight decodes when a row scrolls away or a composable leaves. Requests that complete for a view nobody can see are pure waste, and they arrive in bursts during a fast fling.
- Ask the backend or CDN for a resized variant. Downloading a full-resolution image to show a thumbnail wastes bandwidth as well as memory.
- Prefer WebP or AVIF over PNG, and vector drawables for icons.

Where you see it: bitmaps live in native memory, so watch the graphics and native categories in the Memory Profiler rather than the Java heap alone, and check Play Vitals for the real-user OOM rate.

Measure before cutting: the APK Analyzer in Android Studio breaks a build down by DEX, resources, assets and native libraries, and the answer is usually native code, images, or one oversized dependency.

### The structural wins, roughly in order of payoff
- Ship an Android App Bundle. Play generates per-device splits, so a user downloads one ABI, one density and one language instead of all of them. On an app with native libraries this alone often halves the download.
- Turn on R8 (`minifyEnabled`) and `shrinkResources`. Overly broad keep rules quietly undo both, so read what survived rather than assuming.
- Strip debug symbols from release native libraries and upload the native debug symbols to Play separately, so you still get symbolicated native crashes.
- Convert PNG and JPEG assets to WebP or AVIF, use vector drawables for icons, and stop shipping five densities of the same bitmap when the bundle already splits by density.
- Audit dependencies. The DEX view shows method and byte counts per package; pulling a whole SDK in for one helper function is extremely common.
- Trim what you never use: `androidResources.localeFilters` (the replacement for `resConfigs`) for languages you actually translate, and delete unused assets.
- Play Feature Delivery for a genuinely optional, genuinely large feature — install-time, conditional or on-demand modules. It is not worth the complexity to save a megabyte.

Two things to keep straight. Download size is what the user sees on the store listing and what conversion correlates with, and it is not the size of your APK on disk. And Play caps what a bundle may install at first launch, so anything past that is asset packs or on-demand content, not a compression problem.

They measure three different scales: one function, one user journey, and one real user's session.

- Microbenchmark (`benchmark-junit4`) runs a block of code in a loop on a device with warmup and clock stabilization, and reports nanoseconds per iteration. It answers "is this parser faster than that one". It tells you nothing about frames, startup or how the app feels.
- Macrobenchmark (`benchmark-macro-junit4`) drives the installed app from a separate process with UI Automator and reports `StartupTimingMetric`, `FrameTimingMetric`, `TraceSectionMetric`, `MemoryUsageMetric` and `PowerMetric`. It answers "how long is cold start" and "how janky is this scroll", and it is also what generates baseline profiles.
- JankStats is a library you ship. It reports frame durations from real devices, tagged with whatever state you attach, so you learn which screen janks on the hardware your users actually own — something no lab device tells you.
- Play Vitals and Firebase Performance are the aggregate production view: ANR rate, cold start distribution, crash-free sessions.

### Making the numbers mean anything
- **Benchmark a release-shaped build** — minified and `profileable`, never debuggable. A debug build is interpreted and several times slower, so its numbers are fiction.
- State `CompilationMode` explicitly. `None()` is the worst case, `Partial()` is the baseline-profile case, and `Full()` is a state no real user is in.
- Use a real device with locked clocks. Thermal throttling and emulator noise easily swamp the regression you are hunting.
- Read the median and P90 over many iterations, never a single run.
- Run it in CI on one fixed device and compare against the previous commit, or performance drifts without anyone noticing which change did it.

The system records how your previous process ended, and `ApplicationExitInfo` is how you read that record on the next launch.

Call `activityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons(packageName, 0, 5)` early in `Application.onCreate`, log the newest entry, and attach it to your crash reporter as a breadcrumb. The reasons that come up:
- `REASON_LOW_MEMORY` — the low-memory killer reclaimed you while backgrounded. Extremely common and not a bug in itself.
- `REASON_ANR` — and `getTraceInputStream()` hands you the ANR trace that Play Console would have shown.
- `REASON_CRASH` and `REASON_CRASH_NATIVE` — the second one is the case your JVM crash handler never sees.
- `REASON_USER_REQUESTED` — the user swiped it out of recents. Nothing to fix.
- `REASON_EXCESSIVE_RESOURCE_USAGE`, `REASON_PERMISSION_CHANGE`, `REASON_FREEZER`.
Record `getPss()`, `getRss()` and `getImportance()` alongside: a kill at low importance with a large footprint is a memory problem, not a bug in your restore code.

Most of these reports are not a crash at all. Being killed in the background is normal Android behaviour; what the user notices is that state was lost. So the fix usually lives in restoration — put screen state in `SavedStateHandle` and `rememberSaveable`, restore the navigation back stack, and never keep the only copy of something the user typed in a field of an Activity.

Reproduce it on purpose rather than waiting: `adb shell am kill <package>` kills the process but keeps the task, which is exactly the scenario users hit. Force-stop is a different, harsher thing and is not what you want to test.

To be killed less often, be smaller: the killer sorts by memory footprint, so trim caches in `onTrimMemory`, avoid holding bitmaps and large parsed payloads, and do not hold a foreground service you do not need.

Named trace sections put your methods on the timeline as slices, and a `profileable` manifest flag is what makes a non-debuggable release build traceable at all.

### Instrumenting your code
- `androidx.tracing`'s `trace("LoadFeed") { ... }` opens and closes a slice around the block. The manual `Trace.beginSection` / `endSection` pair has to match on the same thread and survive early returns, which is why the lambda form is the one to use.
- Section names must be string literals and short. R8 does not rewrite them, so they survive minification and stay comparable between releases.
- Use the async form for work that starts on one thread and finishes on another — a request, a coroutine that hops dispatchers. A plain slice around a suspend call ends at the first suspension point, which is rarely what you meant.
- Compose composition tracing (the `tracing-perfetto` artifact plus the compiler option) labels individual composables in the trace, which is how you identify the one recomposing far too often.

### Tracing a release build
- `<profileable android:shell="true" />` in the manifest makes a release build traceable and memory-profileable without making it debuggable. Recent AGP adds it to release builds for you.
- This matters because a debuggable build is interpreted and instrumented; any timing you take from it is meaningless.
- Capture with the System Tracing quick-settings tile, Android Studio's profiler, or `record_android_trace`, then open the result in the Perfetto UI. Start at the frame timeline track, find the janky frames, and read your slices underneath them.

The payoff beyond one investigation: Macrobenchmark's `TraceSectionMetric` turns any of those names into a number, so the same instrumentation becomes a regression test in CI.
